title: Antibacterials II: Protein & Nucleic Acid Synthesis
summary: Ribosomal inhibitors, fluoroquinolones, folate antagonists and others.

lessons.title: Aminoglycosides and Tetracyclines

levels.kid:
Germs build their body parts using tiny machines called **ribosomes**. Ribosomes read instructions and make proteins, like a little factory.

Germ ribosomes are shaped differently from ours. Some antibiotics jam the germ's factory.

**Aminoglycosides** make the factory read the instructions wrong, so the germ builds broken parts and dies. They are strong, but doctors watch the kidneys and ears closely.

**Tetracyclines** like doxycycline stop the factory from getting new pieces. They treat things like tick bites that cause Lyme disease. Milk can stop them from soaking in, so timing matters.
levels.hs:
Both classes target the bacterial **30S ribosomal subunit**, part of the **70S ribosome** that makes proteins. Human ribosomes are **80S**, which gives selectivity.

**Aminoglycosides** (gentamicin, tobramycin, amikacin, streptomycin):
- Cause the ribosome to **misread mRNA**, producing faulty proteins. They are **bactericidal**.
- Mainly for serious **gram-negative** infections, and combined with β-lactams for some heart valve infections (**synergy**).
- Need oxygen to enter bacteria, so they don't work on **anaerobes**.
- Given IV; poorly absorbed by mouth.
- **Toxicity:** **kidney damage** (usually reversible), **ear damage** (hearing loss and balance problems, often permanent) and, rarely, muscle weakness. Blood levels are monitored.

**Tetracyclines** (doxycycline, minocycline, tetracycline):
- Block tRNA from attaching to the ribosome; **bacteriostatic**.
- Used for **Lyme disease**, Rocky Mountain spotted fever, chlamydia, acne, some MRSA skin infections and atypical pneumonia.
- **Bind calcium, iron, magnesium and antacids**, which blocks absorption.
- **Side effects:** sun sensitivity, stomach and esophagus irritation, and **tooth discoloration** in young children. They can rarely raise pressure in the skull.
levels.college:
**Aminoglycosides.** Polycationic aminocyclitols that bind **16S rRNA** at the decoding A site (helix 44), flipping out A1492/A1493 so near-cognate tRNAs are accepted. Misread proteins insert into the membrane, increasing permeability and drug uptake (a positive feedback loop). Uptake requires the **proton motive force** (oxygen-dependent), so anaerobes and acidic, low-oxygen abscesses resist.

**PK/PD:** concentration-dependent killing, long **post-antibiotic effect**, and **adaptive resistance** (reduced uptake after exposure) support extended-interval regimens. Renal elimination; small volume of distribution; poor CSF and bile penetration.

**Uses:** gram-negative sepsis (often as a single empiric add-on), synergy with cell wall agents (enterococcal or streptococcal endocarditis), plague and tularemia (streptomycin, gentamicin), TB (amikacin, streptomycin), inhaled tobramycin in cystic fibrosis, topical/oral neomycin.

**Toxicity:**
- **Nephrotoxicity:** uptake into proximal tubule cells via **megalin**; acute tubular necrosis, non-oliguric, usually reversible. Risk tracks trough exposure.
- **Ototoxicity:** cochlear (hearing loss) and vestibular (gentamicin, streptomycin); irreversible hair cell death; **m.1555A>G** mitochondrial 12S rRNA variant greatly increases susceptibility.
- **Neuromuscular blockade:** reduces presynaptic calcium entry; dangerous in myasthenia gravis and with paralytics.
- Teratogenic (fetal ototoxicity).

**Resistance:** aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes (acetyltransferases, phosphotransferases, nucleotidyltransferases), **16S rRNA methyltransferases** (armA, rmtB: pan-aminoglycoside), efflux. Amikacin and plazomicin resist many modifying enzymes.

**Tetracyclines.** Bind the 30S near the A site, blocking aminoacyl-tRNA accommodation. Doxycycline and minocycline are lipophilic with good tissue penetration. **Glycylcyclines** (tigecycline) and newer agents (omadacycline, eravacycline) evade efflux and ribosomal protection. Adverse: chelation with divalent and trivalent cations, photosensitivity, pill esophagitis, tooth staining and bone deposition, **idiopathic intracranial hypertension**, minocycline vestibular toxicity, hyperpigmentation and drug-induced lupus. Tigecycline carries an all-cause mortality warning. Resistance: efflux (tetA, tetB) and **ribosomal protection proteins** (tetM, tetO).
levels.phd:
**Structural decoding.** Ramakrishnan's crystal structures showed that A1492 and A1493 normally flip out of helix 44 only when a cognate codon-anticodon minihelix forms, sensing Watson-Crick geometry in the minor groove. Aminoglycosides like paromomycin bind inside helix 44 and stabilize the flipped-out state, lowering the energetic penalty for near-cognate pairing and reducing proofreading. Some (gentamicin, neomycin) also bind helix 69 of the 23S rRNA, inhibiting ribosome recycling and translocation.

**Killing mechanism.** Mistranslated membrane proteins trigger the envelope-stress Cpx and Arc two-component systems; whether downstream reactive oxygen species contribute to death (Kohanski and Collins) remains contested, since killing persists anaerobically when uptake is maintained. Uptake depends on the electrical component of the proton motive force; metabolites that boost respiration (alanine, glucose) potentiate killing of persisters, an attractive adjuvant strategy.

**Selectivity and toxicity converge.** Human mitochondrial 12S rRNA resembles bacterial 16S; the m.1555A>G variant makes it more bacterial-like at the drug-binding site, explaining maternally inherited hypersensitivity. Hair cell entry occurs via mechanotransducer channels (TMC1/2) and TRP channels. Designer aminoglycosides with reduced mitochondrial affinity (apramycin derivatives) and otoprotectants (sodium thiosulfate, studied for platinum ototoxicity) are research directions.

**Tetracycline resistance biology.** TetM is a GTPase related to elongation factor G that binds the ribosome and dislodges tetracycline by a conformational change of the h34 region. TetX is a flavin-dependent monooxygenase that inactivates even tigecycline; plasmid-borne tet(X) variants are an emerging threat. Glycylcyclines' bulky 9-position substituent increases ribosomal affinity and sterically clashes with TetM's displacement mechanism.

**Non-antibiotic effects:** tetracyclines inhibit matrix metalloproteinases and microglial activation, the basis for sub-antimicrobial periodontal use and for minocycline neuroprotection trials in stroke and neurodegeneration, which have largely been disappointing.
levels.expert:
**Aminoglycosides on the ward.** Their role has narrowed because of toxicity, but they remain valuable: a single empiric dose in septic shock broadens gram-negative coverage while cultures return; synergy for selected endocarditis; and plague, tularemia and resistant TB. Clinicians use extended-interval strategies with nomogram- or level-guided adjustment, avoid them with other nephrotoxins and in pre-existing kidney disease, and keep courses short. For courses lasting more than a few days, baseline and follow-up **audiometry** are reasonable, and vestibular toxicity (oscillopsia, unsteadiness) should be asked about directly, because hearing tests miss it.

**Neuro relevance:**
- **Myasthenia gravis:** aminoglycosides (along with fluoroquinolones, macrolides and magnesium) can precipitate crisis. Avoid if possible.
- **Neuromuscular blockade** in the operating room is potentiated, causing prolonged paralysis.
- Intrathecal or intraventricular aminoglycosides are reserved for multidrug-resistant gram-negative ventriculitis with a drain.

**Tetracyclines in practice.**
- **Doxycycline** is first-line for Lyme disease, including neuroborreliosis (facial palsy, meningitis, radiculitis), which oral doxycycline treats as well as IV ceftriaxone in trials. It is also first-line for suspected tick-borne rickettsial disease at any age, including young children, because short courses do not cause meaningful tooth staining and delay kills.
- **Idiopathic intracranial hypertension** from tetracyclines (and isotretinoin, vitamin A derivatives) presents with headache and papilledema; combining a tetracycline with isotretinoin for acne is avoided.
- Counsel separation from calcium, iron, magnesium, zinc and antacids, and taking with water while upright to prevent pill esophagitis.
- Minocycline causes dizziness and long-term blue-gray pigmentation; it is less used now.
- Tigecycline is reserved for resistant organisms where alternatives fail, never as monotherapy for bacteremia given low serum levels.

keyPoints: Both target the 30S subunit of the bacterial 70S ribosome
Aminoglycosides cause mRNA misreading; bactericidal, concentration-dependent, oxygen-dependent uptake (no anaerobes)
Aminoglycoside toxicity: nephrotoxicity (reversible), ototoxicity (irreversible), neuromuscular blockade
Tetracyclines block aminoacyl-tRNA binding; bacteriostatic; chelate divalent cations
Tetracycline uses: Lyme, rickettsiae, chlamydia, acne; adverse: photosensitivity, tooth staining, intracranial hypertension

lessons.title: Macrolides, Clindamycin and Linezolid

levels.kid:
The germ's protein factory, the **ribosome**, has two parts: a small one and a big one. These medicines jam the **big part**.

**Macrolides** like azithromycin help with some lung infections and whooping cough.

**Clindamycin** is good against germs that live where there's no air, and it can stop some germs from making poisons.

**Linezolid** is a backup for super tough germs like MRSA and VRE.

Each one has things to watch for. Some can make your heartbeat rhythm a little off, and some can upset your tummy a lot, so doctors choose carefully.
levels.hs:
These drugs block the **50S ribosomal subunit**, the large half of the bacterial ribosome. They are mostly **bacteriostatic**.

**Macrolides** (azithromycin, clarithromycin, erythromycin):
- Treat **"atypical" pneumonia** (*Mycoplasma*, *Legionella*, *Chlamydophila*), **whooping cough** (pertussis), chlamydia and some strep infections in penicillin-allergic patients.
- Side effects: stomach upset (erythromycin makes the gut contract), **QT prolongation** (a heart rhythm risk) and drug interactions (clarithromycin and erythromycin block liver enzymes that clear many drugs).

**Clindamycin:**
- Covers gram-positives (including many MRSA) and **anaerobes**.
- Used for skin infections, dental and jaw infections, and to **turn off toxin production** in severe strep and staph infections.
- Biggest risk: ***C. difficile*** colitis.

**Linezolid:**
- Treats **MRSA** and **VRE** (vancomycin-resistant enterococci), including pneumonia. Works by mouth as well as IV.
- Side effects with longer use: **low platelets and blood counts**, nerve damage, and **serotonin syndrome** when combined with antidepressants like SSRIs.

A classic memory aid: "buy AT 30, CCEL at 50": Aminoglycosides and Tetracyclines at 30S; Clindamycin, Chloramphenicol, Erythromycin (macrolides) and Linezolid at 50S.
levels.college:
**Macrolides** bind the **23S rRNA** in the **nascent peptide exit tunnel** near the peptidyl transferase center, blocking elongation of certain peptide sequences (context-specific arrest rather than a blanket stop).
- **Azithromycin:** huge tissue volume of distribution, concentrated in phagocytes, long half-life allows short courses; little CYP3A4 inhibition.
- **Clarithromycin, erythromycin:** strong **CYP3A4 inhibitors** (raise levels of statins, calcineurin inhibitors, carbamazepine, colchicine); clarithromycin is part of *H. pylori* and *Mycobacterium avium* complex regimens.
- **Erythromycin** is a **motilin receptor agonist**, used deliberately for gastroparesis and to empty the stomach before endoscopy; early infant exposure is linked to **hypertrophic pyloric stenosis**.
- **QT prolongation** via hERG blockade; risk of torsades with other QT drugs, hypokalemia or hypomagnesemia.
- Macrolides also have **immunomodulatory** effects (reduced exacerbations in COPD, bronchiectasis, cystic fibrosis).

**Resistance:** **erm** genes methylate A2058 of 23S rRNA, conferring cross-resistance to macrolides, lincosamides and streptogramin B (**MLSB**). Inducible erm explains why staph that look clindamycin-susceptible may fail; the **D-test** detects this. **mef** encodes efflux (macrolides only).

**Clindamycin** (lincosamide) binds the peptidyl transferase region. Excellent bone and abscess penetration; inhibits exotoxin synthesis (streptococcal toxic shock, necrotizing fasciitis with penicillin). Highest *C. difficile* risk among common antibiotics. Poor CSF penetration but used with pyrimethamine for **cerebral toxoplasmosis** in sulfa allergy.

**Linezolid** (oxazolidinone) binds the 23S A site of the PTC, preventing proper tRNA positioning and **formation of the 70S initiation complex**. Nearly complete oral bioavailability; good CSF penetration. Adverse: **myelosuppression** (thrombocytopenia, duration-dependent), **peripheral and optic neuropathy** and **lactic acidosis** (mitochondrial protein synthesis inhibition), **serotonin syndrome** (reversible weak MAO inhibition). Tedizolid has a similar profile with less marrow toxicity.

**Chloramphenicol:** inhibits peptidyl transferase; dose-related marrow suppression, idiosyncratic aplastic anemia, **gray baby syndrome** (deficient glucuronidation).
levels.phd:
**The exit tunnel is not a passive pipe.** Ribosome profiling and toe-printing showed that macrolides do not block all elongation: certain nascent peptides thread past the drug, while specific motifs (notably +x+ patterns with positively charged residues) trigger stalling. This **context-specific inhibition** means macrolides reshape the proteome rather than shutting it down, explaining bacteriostasis and some pharmacology. The same mechanism regulates resistance: the erm leader peptide (ermCL) stalls in the presence of drug, remodeling mRNA structure to expose the erm ribosome-binding site, so methylase is translated only when macrolide is present: a drug-sensing riboregulator.

**Linezolid and chloramphenicol** are also context-specific, stalling when alanine (and to lesser extent serine or threonine) occupies the penultimate position of the nascent chain, which stabilizes drug binding in the A site. This overturned the textbook view that PTC inhibitors universally block peptide bond formation.

**Mitochondrial toxicity.** Linezolid binds human mitochondrial ribosomes, reducing synthesis of respiratory chain subunits (e.g., COX1). Toxicity tracks cumulative exposure, explaining duration-dependent neuropathy and lactic acidosis. Mitochondrial haplogroups influence susceptibility. Chloramphenicol similarly impairs mitochondrial translation, accounting for reversible marrow suppression.

**Resistance beyond erm.** The **cfr** methyltransferase modifies A2503, conferring the **PhLOPSA** phenotype (phenicols, lincosamides, oxazolidinones, pleuromutilins, streptogramin A) and spreads on plasmids. **optrA** and **poxtA** encode ABC-F proteins that protect the ribosome from oxazolidinones and phenicols, now found in enterococci from animals and humans.

**Immunomodulation.** Macrolides reduce neutrophil IL-8 signaling, alter biofilm quorum sensing in *Pseudomonas* (sub-inhibitory concentrations), and modulate airway mucus, which is the rationale for chronic azithromycin in cystic fibrosis and bronchiectasis despite resistance concerns.
levels.expert:
**How clinicians actually use these drugs.**

**Macrolides:** azithromycin is added to a β-lactam for hospitalized community-acquired pneumonia to cover atypicals. Pneumococcal macrolide resistance is common in the US, so monotherapy is limited to selected outpatients. Before prescribing, check the **QT interval** and interacting drugs; clarithromycin with a statin or colchicine can cause rhabdomyolysis or colchicine toxicity. Macrolides can worsen **myasthenia gravis**.

**Clindamycin:** first add-on in necrotizing soft tissue infection for toxin suppression while surgeons debride. For an MRSA skin abscess, drainage matters most. Always check the D-test when an erythromycin-resistant staph is reported clindamycin-susceptible. Warn every patient about diarrhea and *C. difficile*.

**Linezolid:** an excellent option for MRSA pneumonia, VRE, and CNS infections caused by resistant gram-positives, because of good CSF penetration; post-neurosurgical ventriculitis with VRE or vancomycin failure is a common use. Monitor **complete blood counts weekly** on courses beyond about two weeks; ask about visual change or numbness on long courses (used in drug-resistant TB regimens, where neuropathy is common). **Serotonin syndrome** risk with SSRIs, SNRIs and other serotonergic drugs is real but low; many patients can continue antidepressants with monitoring rather than stopping them abruptly. Watch for hypoglycemia in diabetics on insulin.

**Pitfalls:**
- Azithromycin for every cough: most bronchitis is viral.
- Clindamycin as default for penicillin allergy in surgical prophylaxis: worse surgical site infection rates than cefazolin, which is usually tolerated.
- Linezolid combined with other marrow-suppressing drugs in oncology or transplant patients.
- Forgetting that chloramphenicol, still used globally for meningitis or typhoid where resources are limited, needs blood count monitoring and is avoided in neonates.

Clindamycin: anaerobes, toxin suppression; highest C. difficile risk
Linezolid: MRSA, VRE; myelosuppression, neuropathy, lactic acidosis, serotonin syndrome

lessons.title: Fluoroquinolones

levels.kid:
Germs keep their instructions on a long string called **DNA**. It's so long that it gets twisted, like a phone cord.

Germs have special helpers that untwist the DNA so it can be copied. **Fluoroquinolones**, like ciprofloxacin, jam those helpers. The DNA snaps, and the germ dies.

These medicines are strong and work on lots of germs. But they can sometimes hurt tendons, which connect muscles to bones, and they can upset nerves or the brain. So doctors save them for when they're really the best choice.
levels.hs:
**Fluoroquinolones** (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin) block two bacterial enzymes that manage DNA twisting: **DNA gyrase** (topoisomerase II) and **topoisomerase IV**. When these enzymes are trapped, the bacterial DNA breaks. Fluoroquinolones are **bactericidal**.

**Uses:**
- **Ciprofloxacin:** gram-negatives, including ***Pseudomonas***; urinary infections; anthrax.
- **Levofloxacin and moxifloxacin:** called **"respiratory fluoroquinolones"** because they also cover pneumococcus and atypical pneumonia bugs.
- They are well absorbed by mouth, nearly as well as IV.

**Side effects** (serious enough that they carry boxed warnings):
- **Tendinitis and tendon rupture**, especially the Achilles, and more likely in older adults or people on steroids.
- **Nervous system effects:** confusion, seizures, nerve damage (numbness, tingling) and mood changes.
- **QT prolongation** (heart rhythm risk).
- Blood sugar swings, aortic aneurysm risk, and worsening of **myasthenia gravis**.
- *C. difficile* diarrhea.

Like tetracyclines, they **bind calcium, magnesium and iron**, so antacids and supplements reduce absorption.

Because of these risks, doctors avoid them for simple infections when safer options exist.
levels.college:
**Mechanism.** Type II topoisomerases cut both DNA strands, pass another duplex through and reseal. Fluoroquinolones bind the enzyme-DNA **cleavage complex**, intercalating at the break and stabilizing it; collisions with replication forks convert these into **double-strand breaks**, triggering the SOS response and death. In gram-negatives the main target is **gyrase** (GyrA), in gram-positives **topoisomerase IV** (ParC). A **magnesium-water bridge** links the drug's keto-acid to conserved serine and acidic residues.

**Spectrum by agent:**
- **Ciprofloxacin:** best anti-*Pseudomonas* activity; weak against pneumococcus.
- **Levofloxacin:** gram-negatives (including *Pseudomonas*), pneumococcus, atypicals.
- **Moxifloxacin:** pneumococcus, atypicals, some anaerobes; low urinary concentrations, so not for UTI; less antipseudomonal.
- **Delafloxacin:** anionic, more active in acidic environments, MRSA activity.

**PK:** high oral bioavailability (reduced by chelation with di- and trivalent cations), large volume of distribution, good penetration into prostate, bone and CSF (variable). Cipro and levo are renally cleared; moxi mainly hepatic. Ciprofloxacin inhibits **CYP1A2**, raising theophylline, caffeine, clozapine and tizanidine.

**Adverse effects:**
- **Tendinopathy/rupture:** risk factors age, corticosteroids, renal or solid organ transplant.
- **CNS:** dizziness, insomnia, delirium, psychosis, **seizures** (GABA-A antagonism, enhanced by NSAIDs and theophylline).
- **Peripheral neuropathy**, potentially persistent.
- **QT prolongation** (moxi > levo > cipro).
- Dysglycemia, **aortic aneurysm and dissection**, retinal detachment association.
- **Myasthenia gravis exacerbation** (boxed warning).
- Phototoxicity; arthropathy in juvenile animals, so use in children is limited to specific indications.

**Resistance:** chromosomal mutations in the **quinolone resistance-determining regions** of *gyrA* and *parC*, efflux upregulation, porin loss, and plasmid genes (*qnr* target protection, **aac(6')-Ib-cr** acetylation, qepA/oqxAB efflux).
levels.phd:
**Poisons, not inhibitors.** Fluoroquinolones are topoisomerase **poisons**: rather than reducing enzyme activity, they convert an essential enzyme into a DNA-damaging agent. Crystal structures (Laponogov, Bax and colleagues) show two drug molecules intercalated at the cleaved scissile phosphates, four base pairs apart, with the C3/C4 keto-acid coordinating a noncatalytic Mg²⁺ held by water molecules to Ser83 and Asp87 (E. coli GyrA numbering). Mutations at these residues (Ser83Leu, Asp87Asn) break the bridge, explaining why they dominate clinical resistance. Novel bacterial topoisomerase inhibitors (NBTIs) and **gepotidacin** (a triazaacenaphthylene) bind a distinct pocket, retain activity against quinolone-resistant strains and act on both enzymes in a balanced way, reducing single-step resistance; gepotidacin has been approved for uncomplicated UTI.

**Lethality has two arms.** At lower concentrations, killing requires protein synthesis (blocked by chloramphenicol); at higher concentrations, killing becomes protein-synthesis independent, attributed to chromosome fragmentation by dissociation of gyrase subunits from DNA. The SOS response not only repairs damage but induces error-prone polymerases, increasing mutation rates and horizontal transfer, so sub-lethal exposure can accelerate resistance to other drugs.

**Selectivity and toxicity.** Human topoisomerase II is far less sensitive, but quinolones chelate metals and inhibit matrix metalloproteinase-regulating pathways in tendons and in aortic wall collagen, plausibly underlying tendinopathy and aneurysm. Mitochondrial toxicity and oxidative stress in neurons, and GABA-A antagonism linked to the C7 substituent (piperazine), explain CNS effects; the structure-activity relationships let chemists tune spectrum, phototoxicity (C8 halogen) and seizure liability.

**Mutant prevention concentration** was largely developed with quinolones: single gyrA mutants are selected readily in the window between MIC and MPC, informing exposure targets.
levels.expert:
**Use them deliberately, not reflexively.** Regulators restricted fluoroquinolones for uncomplicated sinusitis, bronchitis and cystitis because the disabling effects (tendon, nerve, CNS) outweigh benefit when alternatives exist. Where they shine:
- Oral step-down for gram-negative bacteremia, pyelonephritis or prostatitis, given high bioavailability.
- *Pseudomonas* when an oral option is needed (ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin).
- Respiratory infections in patients with severe β-lactam allergy.
- Bone and joint infection combinations (with rifampin for staphylococcal prosthetic infection).
- Anthrax and plague.

**Neurology-relevant warnings:**
- **Delirium and seizures** in older adults, patients with prior seizures, structural brain lesions or renal impairment; check co-medications (theophylline, NSAIDs).
- **Myasthenia gravis:** avoid; they can precipitate respiratory failure.
- **Peripheral neuropathy** can be early and persistent; stop the drug at first symptoms.
- **QT:** check baseline ECG when combined with antipsychotics, antiemetics or other QT-prolonging drugs, and correct potassium and magnesium.

**Practical counseling:** take apart from calcium, iron, zinc, magnesium and antacids; avoid strenuous exercise if tendon pain develops and report it; avoid excessive sun.

**Resistance reality:** many *E. coli* urinary isolates and most gonorrhea are now resistant; empiric use for gonorrhea is obsolete. Prior fluoroquinolone exposure in the last few months predicts resistance; choose another empiric class.

**Pediatrics:** generally avoided, but used when benefits clearly outweigh risk (complicated UTI with resistant organisms, cystic fibrosis exacerbations, anthrax).

**Interaction checklist:** ciprofloxacin raises tizanidine (contraindicated), theophylline and clozapine through CYP1A2; all can enhance warfarin effect.

lessons.title: Sulfonamides and Trimethoprim

levels.kid:
Germs need a vitamin called **folate** to build new DNA and grow. We get folate from food, but many germs have to make their own, like baking their own bread.

**Sulfa drugs** and **trimethoprim** each block a different step in the germ's bread recipe. Together, they're like taking away the flour AND the oven. Doctors often give them as a team.

They help with bladder infections and some skin and lung infections.

Some people get a rash from sulfa drugs, which can rarely be serious, so they tell the doctor right away.
levels.hs:
Bacteria must **make their own folate** (needed to build DNA), while humans get it from food. That difference is the target.

- **Sulfonamides** (like **sulfamethoxazole**) look like **PABA**, a folate building block, and block the enzyme **dihydropteroate synthase**.
- **Trimethoprim** blocks **dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR)** a few steps later. Bacterial DHFR is much more sensitive than human DHFR.

Given together as **TMP-SMX** (trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole), they block two steps in a row (**sequential blockade**), and the combination is bactericidal.

**Uses:**
- **Urinary tract infections** (where local resistance allows).
- **MRSA skin infections**.
- **Pneumocystis pneumonia (PJP)** treatment and prevention in people with weak immune systems, such as HIV or after transplant.
- Prevention of **toxoplasmosis**, and *Nocardia* and *Stenotrophomonas* infections.

**Side effects:**
- **Allergic rashes**, rarely severe skin reactions (Stevens-Johnson syndrome).
- **High potassium** and a rise in creatinine (trimethoprim affects the kidneys).
- **Hemolysis** (red cell breakdown) in people with **G6PD deficiency**.
- Not used in newborns or late pregnancy: sulfa can push bilirubin into a baby's brain (**kernicterus**).
- Interactions, especially boosting the blood thinner **warfarin**.
levels.college:
**Folate pathway.** GTP → dihydropteridine; **dihydropteroate synthase (DHPS)** condenses it with **PABA** to form dihydropteroate → dihydrofolate (DHF) → **DHFR** reduces DHF to **tetrahydrofolate (THF)**, the one-carbon donor for thymidylate, purines and methionine. Humans lack DHPS (dietary folate is taken up by transporters).

**Sulfonamides** are PABA structural analogs; they compete at DHPS and can be incorporated as dead-end pterin-sulfonamide adducts. Bacteriostatic alone. **Trimethoprim** binds bacterial DHFR roughly tens of thousands of times more tightly than human DHFR. The combination is synergistic and often bactericidal.

**Relatives:** **pyrimethamine** (protozoal DHFR; with sulfadiazine for toxoplasmosis), **dapsone** (a sulfone; leprosy, PJP prophylaxis; methemoglobinemia and hemolysis), **sulfasalazine** (colon releases sulfapyridine and 5-ASA), **silver sulfadiazine** (burns).

**Adverse effects:**
- **Hypersensitivity:** maculopapular rash (very common in HIV), **SJS/TEN**, DRESS, drug fever. Mediated partly by reactive **hydroxylamine and nitroso metabolites** of the arylamine N4 group.
- **Hyperkalemia:** trimethoprim blocks **ENaC** in the collecting duct (amiloride-like).
- **Creatinine rise without GFR loss:** trimethoprim inhibits tubular creatinine secretion (OCT2/MATE).
- **Hematologic:** hemolysis in G6PD deficiency, megaloblastic anemia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia.
- **Kernicterus** in neonates (bilirubin displacement from albumin).
- Aseptic meningitis (rare), hypoglycemia, hyponatremia.
- **Interactions:** CYP2C9 inhibition by sulfamethoxazole raises **warfarin** and phenytoin; additive hyperkalemia with ACE inhibitors, ARBs, spironolactone; additive antifolate toxicity with methotrexate.

**Leucovorin** (folinic acid) bypasses DHFR in human cells and is given with pyrimethamine to protect the marrow; bacteria cannot take it up efficiently.

**Resistance:** plasmid-borne alternative enzymes (**sul1/sul2/sul3** DHPS, **dfr** DHFR variants), chromosomal target mutations, and overproduction of PABA.
levels.phd:
**Historical arc.** Prontosil (Domagk, 1935) was the first synthetic systemic antibacterial; the Tréfouëls showed it is a prodrug cleaved in vivo to sulfanilamide. The 1937 "Elixir Sulfanilamide" disaster, in which diethylene glycol solvent killed over a hundred people, led directly to the 1938 US Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act requiring safety proof before marketing.

**Structural selectivity of trimethoprim.** Trimethoprim's diaminopyrimidine forms a salt bridge with a conserved acidic residue (Asp27 in E. coli DHFR); its trimethoxybenzyl group exploits a hydrophobic pocket shape that differs in vertebrate DHFR (where Phe31 and other residues alter the pocket). Methotrexate, by contrast, binds both tightly. Resistance mutations (chromosomal *folA* promoter changes and substitutions such as Leu28Arg) trade affinity for catalytic efficiency, and Toprak's morbidostat experiments mapped repeatable, ordered mutational trajectories.

**Sulfonamide resistance enzymes** (Sul1–3) are DHPS homologs containing a Phe-Gly insertion in the PABA-binding loop that discriminates against the sulfonamide's sulfonyl group while preserving PABA binding: a striking example of selective substrate discrimination achieved by a two-residue insertion (shown in 2023 crystal structures).

**Is the synergy real in vivo?** Theoretical sequential blockade predicts synergy; experimentally, mutual potentiation also arises because THF depletion reduces the pterin supply, feeding back on DHPS (a cyclic pathway model proposed by Minato and colleagues). Many isolates resistant to one component remain inhibited by the combination.

**Hypersensitivity immunology.** CYP2C9 oxidizes sulfamethoxazole to the hydroxylamine, which auto-oxidizes to nitroso-sulfamethoxazole that haptenates proteins; glutathione depletion (as in advanced HIV) increases reactive metabolite burden. HLA associations (e.g., HLA-B*13:01 with dapsone hypersensitivity) enable genotype screening in some populations.

**The "sulfa allergy" myth.** Non-antibiotic sulfonamides (furosemide, thiazides, acetazolamide, celecoxib, sumatriptan) lack the N4 arylamine and the N1 heterocycle implicated in antibiotic reactions; cross-reactivity data suggest that people with sulfonamide antibiotic allergy are generally more reactive to other drugs, not specifically to sulfonamide-containing ones.
levels.expert:
**TMP-SMX at the bedside.**
- **PJP:** first-line treatment and prophylaxis. Prophylaxis is standard in HIV with low CD4 counts, after organ or stem-cell transplant, and with prolonged high-level corticosteroids plus other immunosuppressants, which includes some neuro-oncology patients on dexamethasone with temozolomide. It also prevents toxoplasma reactivation.
- **Cerebral toxoplasmosis** (ring-enhancing lesions in advanced HIV): pyrimethamine with sulfadiazine and leucovorin is classic; TMP-SMX is an accepted alternative and more available. A neurosurgeon may be asked about biopsy if lesions fail to respond in about two weeks.
- **Nocardia**, including brain abscess: TMP-SMX-based combinations, often with neurosurgical drainage.
- **MRSA skin abscesses:** TMP-SMX after drainage improves cure rates.

**Monitoring and pitfalls:**
- Check **potassium and creatinine**, especially in older adults on ACE inhibitors, ARBs or spironolactone; hyperkalemia causes hospitalizations and sudden death in this group.
- A creatinine bump on trimethoprim may be secretion blockade rather than kidney injury; cystatin C or clinical context helps distinguish.
- Check **INR** soon after starting in patients on warfarin; this is one of the most dangerous common interactions.
- **Phenytoin** levels rise.
- In HIV, rash on TMP-SMX is common; mild rashes can sometimes be "treated through" with close watching, or desensitized, given how valuable the drug is. Mucosal involvement, blistering or fever means stop immediately (possible SJS/TEN).
- Test **G6PD** before dapsone or primaquine; consider it with TMP-SMX in high-risk ancestry.

**Allergy labels:** a non-severe sulfonamide antibiotic reaction does not contraindicate thiazides, loop diuretics, acetazolamide or sumatriptan. Avoid unnecessary substitution that leads to worse therapy.

keyPoints: Bacteria synthesize folate; humans absorb it from diet
Sulfonamides are PABA analogs blocking dihydropteroate synthase; trimethoprim blocks bacterial DHFR
TMP-SMX: UTI, MRSA skin, PJP treatment/prophylaxis, toxoplasmosis prophylaxis, Nocardia
Toxicity: rash/SJS, hyperkalemia (ENaC block), creatinine rise, G6PD hemolysis, kernicterus, warfarin interaction
Leucovorin bypasses DHFR to protect human cells (e.g., with pyrimethamine)

lessons.title: Metronidazole and Others

levels.kid:
Some germs live where there's no air, like deep inside a wound or in the gut. **Metronidazole** is great at beating these no-air germs.

It's sneaky: the medicine is harmless until the germ itself switches it on. Then it breaks the germ's DNA.

It also fights some tiny one-celled critters that cause tummy bugs.

**Nitrofurantoin** is a medicine that gathers in pee, so it's good for bladder infections.

**Colistin** is an old, last-resort medicine for super tough germs. It's strong but can hurt the kidneys, so it's saved for emergencies.
levels.hs:
**Metronidazole** is a **nitroimidazole**. It is a **prodrug**: it becomes active only inside **anaerobic** organisms (which live without oxygen), where it is chemically reduced into reactive pieces that **damage DNA**. It is bactericidal.

**Uses:**
- **Anaerobic bacteria** like *Bacteroides fragilis*, in abdominal infections and **brain abscesses** (it gets into the brain well).
- **Protozoa**: *Giardia*, *Entamoeba histolytica* (amebic dysentery and liver abscess), *Trichomonas*.
- **Bacterial vaginosis** and part of some *H. pylori* regimens.

**Side effects:** metallic taste, nausea, dark urine, and with long use **nerve damage** (numbness) or, rarely, problems with balance and coordination from effects on the **cerebellum**. Patients are told to avoid alcohol during treatment. It increases the effect of warfarin.

**Other antibacterials:**
- **Nitrofurantoin:** concentrates in urine; used only for **bladder infections**. Long-term use can rarely damage the lungs or liver.
- **Fosfomycin:** a single-step oral option for some bladder infections.
- **Polymyxins** (**colistin**, polymyxin B): disrupt the outer membrane of gram-negative bacteria. Last-resort drugs for **carbapenem-resistant** bacteria; they can harm the kidneys and nerves.
- **Fidaxomicin:** a narrow drug for ***C. difficile*** that spares other gut bacteria and lowers relapse.
- **Rifampin:** blocks bacterial RNA polymerase; used in TB and in combinations for staph infections of implants.
levels.college:
**Metronidazole.** Enters cells by passive diffusion; in anaerobes and microaerophiles, low-redox-potential electron carriers (**ferredoxin**, reduced by **pyruvate:ferredoxin oxidoreductase**, PFOR) reduce its **nitro group** to short-lived nitro radical anions and hydroxylamine intermediates that cause DNA strand breaks and helix destabilization. Aerobic human cells lack the low-potential reductants, and oxygen reoxidizes the radical (futile cycling), giving selectivity.

**PK:** near-complete oral bioavailability; excellent tissue penetration including **CSF and brain abscess**; hepatic metabolism.

**Adverse effects:** metallic taste, GI upset, **peripheral neuropathy** with prolonged courses, **metronidazole-induced encephalopathy** (ataxia, dysarthria, confusion; symmetric T2/FLAIR hyperintensity of the **dentate nuclei**, splenium and brainstem; reversible on stopping), seizures and aseptic meningitis (rare). A disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol is traditionally warned about, although controlled data are weak. Inhibits CYP2C9 (warfarin potentiation). Resistance: reduced PFOR activity, *nim* genes (nitroimidazole reductases forming non-toxic amines), efflux. **Tinidazole** and **secnidazole** are longer-acting relatives.

**Nitrofurantoin:** reduced by bacterial flavoproteins to reactive intermediates damaging ribosomes, DNA and metabolic enzymes; multiple targets make resistance rare. Achieves therapeutic levels only in urine; avoid with significantly reduced GFR (inadequate urine levels, toxicity). Adverse: acute hypersensitivity pneumonitis, chronic **pulmonary fibrosis**, hepatitis, neuropathy, hemolysis in G6PD deficiency.

**Polymyxins:** cationic lipopeptides that displace Mg²⁺ and Ca²⁺ bridging **lipid A** of LPS, permeabilizing outer and inner membranes. Inactive against gram-positives, *Proteus*, *Serratia*, *Burkholderia*. **Nephrotoxicity** (acute tubular necrosis) and **neurotoxicity** (paresthesias, neuromuscular blockade, apnea). Colistin is given as an inactive prodrug (colistimethate). Resistance: lipid A modification with phosphoethanolamine or aminoarabinose; plasmid **mcr-1**.

**Fidaxomicin:** macrocycle inhibiting RNA polymerase switch-region opening; minimal absorption, narrow spectrum, fewer *C. difficile* recurrences. **Rifamycins** bind the RNA polymerase β-subunit (rpoB); never monotherapy because resistance emerges rapidly.
levels.phd:
**Reductive activation as selectivity filter.** The one-electron reduction potential of metronidazole is very negative (around −486 mV), below what aerobic electron carriers achieve but within reach of ferredoxins and flavodoxins of anaerobes. Under air, the nitro radical anion transfers its electron to O₂, regenerating parent drug and producing superoxide, which explains reduced aerobic activity. In *Helicobacter pylori*, activation depends on the oxygen-insensitive NADPH nitroreductase **RdxA**; null mutations cause resistance, which is common worldwide and drives regimen choice.

**Neurotoxicity biology.** Proposed mechanisms include modulation of inhibitory GABA receptors in cerebellar and vestibular neurons, axonal swelling from reactive intermediates binding neuronal RNA, and thiamine antagonism (metronidazole can be converted to a thiamine analog by thiaminase activity). The predilection for the dentate nucleus parallels other toxic-metabolic encephalopathies affecting highly metabolically active nuclei.

**Polymyxin pharmacology** is a cautionary tale. Licensed in the 1950s before modern PK methods, colistin dosing was guided by little data and abandoned because of toxicity, then resurrected for carbapenem-resistant organisms. Population PK studies (Nation, Li and colleagues) showed that colistimethate's slow conversion leads to delayed active concentrations and narrow therapeutic windows, and that polymyxin B (given as active drug, non-renally cleared) achieves more predictable exposure. Heteroresistance and rapid regrowth make monotherapy unreliable.

**mcr-1** (described in China in 2015) encodes a phosphoethanolamine transferase on conjugative plasmids, linked to agricultural colistin use; its discovery led several countries to ban colistin as a livestock growth promoter.

**Fidaxomicin's structural mechanism** (Lin, Darst and colleagues, 2018) binds the RNA polymerase clamp and the σ-factor region, locking the clamp open and preventing promoter DNA from entering, a mechanism distinct from rifamycins, which block the RNA exit channel after a few nucleotides. Its narrow spectrum preserves *Bacteroidetes* and colonization resistance, the likely basis of lower recurrence.
levels.expert:
**Metronidazole in neurosurgery and neurology.** Standard empiric therapy for **brain abscess** of unknown source is a third-generation cephalosporin plus metronidazole (adding vancomycin after neurosurgery or trauma), because anaerobes and streptococci (oral, sinus, otogenic sources) dominate. Aspiration or excision both diagnoses and treats; courses run for weeks with serial imaging. Long courses raise the risk of **neuropathy** and **cerebellar encephalopathy**; ask about numbness and gait, and if a patient develops new ataxia or dysarthria on therapy, think of the drug before assuming abscess progression. MRI showing symmetric dentate nucleus signal is the clue, and it resolves after stopping.

**C. difficile:** guidelines now favor oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin; metronidazole is reserved for mild disease when those are unavailable. Fidaxomicin reduces recurrence; bezlotoxumab (anti-toxin B antibody) and fecal microbiota-based therapies address recurrent disease.

**Nitrofurantoin:** excellent for uncomplicated cystitis with low resistance, but useless for pyelonephritis or bacteremia (no tissue levels). Avoid in significant renal impairment and in late pregnancy near term (neonatal hemolysis). Chronic prophylaxis in older adults warrants vigilance for cough and dyspnea.

**Polymyxins:** reserved for carbapenem-resistant gram-negatives when newer β-lactam combinations are unavailable or inactive; outcomes were worse than ceftazidime-avibactam in comparative studies. Monitor creatinine closely; avoid with aminoglycosides and other nephrotoxins. Intraventricular polymyxin can be used for multidrug-resistant *Acinetobacter* ventriculitis with a drain, coordinated with neurosurgery.

**Rifampin:** added for staphylococcal prosthetic device infection with retained hardware (spinal instrumentation, prosthetic joints) because it penetrates biofilm; always combined, and started only after bacteremia clears. Its powerful CYP induction (anticoagulants, antiseizure drugs, hormonal contraceptives, immunosuppressants) is the main practical hazard.

keyPoints: Metronidazole is a prodrug activated by anaerobic ferredoxin reduction, damaging DNA
Uses: anaerobes (brain abscess, abdominal), Giardia, Entamoeba, Trichomonas, bacterial vaginosis
Metronidazole toxicity: metallic taste, neuropathy, cerebellar encephalopathy (dentate nuclei on MRI), warfarin interaction
Nitrofurantoin: cystitis only; pulmonary toxicity; avoid with low GFR
Polymyxins disrupt LPS (lipid A); last resort for CRE; nephro- and neurotoxic; mcr-1 resistance
